blocks.text: But the aljarbuo is also said to devise something else. It sometimes covers its windows, or more truly its holes, with earth at the very surface, so that they do not appear from the outside ^{(10)}. In Arabic this is called دم [damma] damma. Alcamus: دم اليربوع حجره غطاه وسواه [damma l-yarbūʿu ḥujrahu ghaṭṭāhu wa-sawwāhu] Damma aljarbuo its burrow, that is, it covered it and leveled it. Whence the burrow also has the name دممة [dummama] dumama. The same Alcamus: الدممة حجرة اليربوع وتراب يجمعه اليربوع ويخرجه من الحجر فيسوي به بابه [al-dummamatu ḥujratu l-yarbūʿi wa-turābun yajmaʿuhu l-yarbūʿu wa-yukhrijuhu mina l-ḥujri fa-yusawwī bihi bābahu] Dumama, the burrow of the aljarbuo, and the earth which it gathers and digs out from its burrow, so as to level its entrance with it. Accordingly, just as the hole of its burrow covered with earth is called نافقا [nāfiqāʾ] naphika, by a metaphor taken from this, نافق [nāfaqa] naphaka, a verb of the third conjugation, means to dissemble in religion, and to profess one thing with the mouth while keeping another hidden in the mind. And منافق [munāfiq] munaphik is a hypocrite. Damir: ظاهر بيته تراب وباطنه حفر وكذلك المنافق ظاهره ايمان وباطنه كفر [ẓāhiru baytihi turābun wa-bāṭinuhu ḥafrun wa-kadhālika l-munāfiqu ẓāhiruhu īmānun wa-bāṭinuhu kufrun] The outer part of its house is earth, but the inner part is hollow. A hypocrite likewise has faith on the outside, but infidelity on the inside. Algiahid, and others: واسم المنافق لم يكن في الجاهلية لكن لمن اسر الكفر واظهر الايمان [wa-smu l-munāfiqi lam yakun fī l-jāhiliyyati lākin li-man asarra l-kufra wa-aẓhara l-īmāna] The name munaphik did not exist in Paganism, but is (said) of him who conceals infidelity and displays faith. Albazi: تعالي اشتق له هذا الاسم من هذا الاصل وهو من نافقا اليربوع لانه لما ابطن الكفر [col. 1013] واظهر الايمان [taʿālā shtaqqa lahu hādhā l-isma min hādhā l-aṣli wa-huwa min nāfiqāʾi l-yarbūʿi li-annahu lammā abṭana l-kufra wa-aẓhara l-īmāna] God Most High derived the name of the hypocrite from this root, namely from naphika, or the hole of the mouse called aljarbuo; because inside is infidelity, and outside is faith. The Arabs say these and many other things on Azoara 73 of the Qur'an, whose title is المنافقون [al-munāfiqūn] the hypocrites. In Alcamus the nest of this animal is called لغز [lughz] [II, 424] logoz, as if you should say labyrinth, because in nests of this sort the paths are winding and very intricate. And accordingly in Arabic الغاز [alghāz] algaz is the name for طرق تلطوي وتشكل علي مسالكها [ṭuruqun taltawwī wa-tushkilu ʿalā masālikihā] paths which in their course are twisted and entangled. To this kind of mouse must be referred what Synesius says about a certain commander John toward the end of Epistle 104: Δίκην ἀρουραίου μυὸς ἐνεδεδύκει τῇ πέτρᾳ [Dikēn arouraiou myos enededykei tē petra], Like a field mouse he had hidden himself in the rock, that is, in Bombaea, a most heavily fortified stronghold in the hollow of a cliff. For other field mice do not nest in rock, but only the aljarbuo ^{(11)}. Which these words of Ibnolgiauzi prove: اليربوع لا يتخذ بيته الا في موضع صلب مرتفع ليسلم من سيل او حافر ثم لا يجعلة الا عند اكمة او شجرة او صخرة ليلا يضل اذا عاد اليه [al-yarbūʿu lā yattakhidhu baytahu illā fī mawḍiʿin ṣulbin murtafiʿin li-yaslama min saylin aw ḥāfirin thumma lā yajʿaluhu illā ʿinda akamatin aw shajaratin aw ṣakhratin li-allā yaḍilla idhā ʿāda ilayhi] The aljarbuo does not prepare its house except in a hard (that is, rocky) and elevated place, so that it may be safe from the inrush of waters and from the hoof (of horses). Nor does it set it up except by mounds, or trees, or rocks, lest it lose its way when it returns to it. Which happens especially to the young of this little animal. Whence the proverb in Damir: اضل من ولد اليربوع [aḍallu min waladi l-yarbūʿi] He wanders more than the young of the aljarbuo, about one who roams and never fixes his foot anywhere. In the same place: وفي طباعه انه اذا مشي في ارض سهلة او لينة مشي علي موخر كفه حتي لا يعرف اثر وطيه كما يفعل الارنب [wa-fī ṭibāʿihi annahu idhā mashā fī arḍin sahlatin aw layyinatin mashā ʿalā muʾakhkhari kaffihi ḥattā lā yuʿrafa atharu waṭʾihi kamā yafʿalu l-arnabu] It is also part of its nature that, when it walks on soft and tender earth, it treads on the tips of its feet, so that its tracks may not be recognized in the places on which it has stepped: which is also customary for the hare. Likewise: وهو [II, 425] يجتر ويبعر وله كرش واسنان واضراس من الفك الاعلي والاسفلي [wa-huwa yajtarru wa-yabʿaru wa-lahu kirshun wa-asnānun wa-aḍrāsun mina l-fakki l-aʿlā wa-l-asfalī] It also ruminates, and voids dung, and has a paunch (after the manner of ruminants); although it has front teeth and molars in both the upper and the lower jaw. Peculiar to this same mouse is the fact that it leaps. The Arabs express this by the most proper verb بحظل [baḥẓala] bachdala. Alcamus: بحظل قفز قفزان اليربوع [baḥẓala qafaza qafazāna l-yarbūʿi] Bachdala, he leaped with the leap of the aljarbuo. So also Giauhari. Which very thing Theophrastus observed above concerning those mice which walk on two feet: Ὅταν δὲ διώκωνται, πηδῶσι· [Hotan de diōkōntai, pēdōsi] If anyone pursues them, they leap. In its burrows nests a kind of snake which the Arabs call جنادع [janādiʿ] gianadio, or جنادب [janādib] gianadibo. Alcamus: الجنادع الاجناش اوجنادب تكون في حجرة اليرابيع [al-janādiʿu l-aḥnāshu aw janādibu takūnu fī ḥujrati l-yarābīʿi] Algianadio, (a kind of) serpents or gia- [col. 1014] nadibo: these are in the nest of the aljarabii, which is the plural of the word اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo. If the aljarbuo mates with a common mouse, the hybrid mouse born from this is called فرنب [farnab] pharnab, or phirnib. Alcamus: الفرنب الفارة او ولدها من اليربوع [al-farnabu l-fāratu aw waladuhā mina l-yarbūʿi] Alpharnab (or alphirnib), a mouse, or its offspring by the aljarbuo. This too is peculiar to it, that the aljarbuo is eaten by the Arabs, whereas the eating of a mouse is otherwise forbidden to them. Damir in the chapter الفار [al-fār] alphar, that is, On the mouse: يحرم اكل جميع انواع الفار الا اليربوع [yaḥrumu aklu jamīʿi anwāʿi l-fāri illā l-yarbūʿa] The eating of all species of mouse is prohibited, except the aljarbuo. Yet there is some disagreement among the Arabs on this matter. For according to the opinion of Abuchanipha: لا يوكل لانه من الحشرات [lā yuʾkalu li-annahu mina l-ḥasharāti] It (the aljarbuo) is not eaten, because it is one of the subterranean animals. And Algazali, in the book entitled الوسيط [al-wasīṭ] The Mediator, denies that anything is to be eaten من الحشرات الا الضب [mina l-ḥasharāti illā l-ḍabba] of the subterranean animals except the land crocodile. Yet by others there are excepted in addition اليربوع وابن عرس وام حبين والقنفد والدلدل [al-yarbūʿu wa-bnu ʿirsin wa-ummu ḥubaynin wa-l-qunfudhu wa-l-duldulu] the aljarbuo, and the weasel, and the chameleon, and the hedgehog, and the porcupine. Hence Damir says of the aljarbuo: يحل اكله لان العرب تستطيبه وتحله [yaḥillu akluhu li-anna l-ʿaraba tastaṭībuhu wa-tuḥilluhu] The eating of it is permitted, because the Arabs allow it and take delight in it. Thus indeed the great Canonists of the Arabs define it: Ata, and Achmed Ben-Hantal, and Ibnolmandsar, and Abutsaur, etc. Accordingly, not only the aljarbuo, but also its burrow is bought, that is, the right of probing and searching it in order to catch this animal in it. Which, however, because it mostly succeeds poorly, has passed into a proverb among the Arabs; as when they say, كالمشتري القاصعا باليربوع [ka-l-mushtarī l-qāṣiʿāʾa bi-l-yarbūʿi] Like one who in exchange for [II, 426] an aljarbuo buys its hole. Which proverb يضرب الذي يدع العين ويتبع الاثر [yuḍrabu lladhī yadaʿu l-ʿayna wa-yattabiʿu l-athara] strikes at him who, leaving the reality behind, follows only the trace. In Greek you would say, Σκιὰν ἀντὶ τοῦ σώματος [Skian anti tou sōmatos], A shadow instead of the body. And here too the Arabs are fastidious, and to the other mice of this kind they prefer the Suphariensian, which Alcamus describes thus: يربوع شفاري ضخم الاذنين وطويلهما العاري البراثين ولا يلحق سريعا والطويل والغوايم الرخو اللحم الدسم [yarbūʿun shufāriyyun ḍakhmu l-udhunayni wa-ṭawīluhumā l-ʿārī l-barāthīni wa-lā yulḥaqu sarīʿan wa-l-ṭawīlu wa-l-qawāʾimi l-rakhwu l-laḥmi l-dasimu] The Suphariensian jarbuo has thick and long ears, is bare of claws so that it does not easily take hold, with long legs, and tender and fat flesh. In Abenbitar: يربوع الاسراييلي لحم اليربوع يقد وغذا كثير ويلين البطن [yarbūʿun al-isrāʾīliyyu laḥmu l-yarbūʿi yuqaddu wa-ghidhāʾun kathīrun wa-yulayyinu l-baṭna] The Israelite jarbuo is what the flesh of the aljarbuo is called when it is dried. Moreover, it is of much nourishment, and softens the belly. To dry in Arabic is قد [qadda] kadda, which properly signifies [col. 1015] to expose flesh, sliced lengthwise, to the wind, just as among us to smoke, so that the moisture may be consumed. Whence both the hedgehog and the aljarbuo are called قداد [qudād] kedad, because each animal is dried in this way. Alcamus: القداد القنفد واليربوع [al-qudādu l-qunfudhu wa-l-yarbūʿu] Alkedado, the hedgehog and the Aljarbuo. In the Arabic versions of the Sacred text the word aljarbuo occurs only once in all, namely in Es. LXVI, 17, where the Arabic translator has it thus: الذين ياكلون لحم الخنازير والرذالات واليربوع [alladhīna yaʾkulūna laḥma l-khanāzīri wa-l-radhālāti wa-l-yarbūʿa] Who eat swine's flesh, and abominations, and the Aljarbua, that is, the species for the genus. For the Hebrew has והעכבר, and the mouse. But the Arab did not lack a reason why he should render it اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbua. For we have already shown that in the whole genus of mice this one alone is edible among the Arabs. Besides, although עכבר achbar for the Hebrews signifies a mouse in general, yet in Arabic this very word عكبر [ʿakbar] achbar, in the plural عكابر [ʿakābir] achabiro, signifies the male of the اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo. Alcamus: العكابر ذكور من اليرابيع [al-ʿakābiru dhukūrun mina l-yarābīʿi] Alachabiro, the males of the Aljarabii: which we have already said is the plural of the word اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo. Therefore, while اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] is the name of the species, العكبر [al-ʿakbar] alachbar signifies the male, just as العطيوطة [al-ʿaṭyūṭa] alatiuta signifies the female. Alcamus: العطيوطة اليربوع الانثي [al-ʿaṭyūṭatu l-yarbūʿu l-unthā] Alatiuta, the female Aljarbuo. Teixeira the Portuguese calls them ratones del mato, that is, mice of the thicket, and describes them in these words in chapter 4 of his Indicum itinerarium: Son estos ratones del grandor de los grandes nuestros communes, tienen el pelo pardo tirante à blanco. Tienen de raton las orejas, manos, y la cola: cuya punta, y los ojos, y cabeça, son de conejo; y las piernas como de gazela. Corren mucho saltando, hazen cueua como conejo. Y ay dellos grande quantidad [II, 427] por aquel de sierto. Los Arabes los comen, y dizen, que son muy buenos. That is: These mice are equal in size to the largest of our common ones, of an ash-gray color. They have the ears, forefeet, and tail of a mouse; the tip of which, and the eyes and head, are those of a rabbit; and the haunches (that is, the hind legs) are those of a roe deer. They mostly run by leaping, and they dig burrows like rabbits. Of these in that desert (in the part of Arabia neighboring Babylonia) there is a very great abundance. The Arabs use them for food, and assert that they are of the best flavor. By which words the aljarbuo is entirely described, as everyone will admit. Concerning the same animal, Olearius writes thus in book 6 of his Itinerarium Persicum, page 64: We saw near Terkin (in Circassia) a kind of field mouse, called in Arabic IERBUA. It has the size of a squirrel, and is not dissimilar in shape; its fur, however, is darker; and it has the head of a mouse; long ears; legs short in front, longer behind. Accordingly they cannot run except uphill; on level ground they almost creep along, or by a leap they are carried up above the earth to five or six feet. The tail is long, resting on the back, hairless on the stem, bushy and whitish at the tip. To see many of them springing upward with the same impulse was a pleasant spectacle. They say that Babylonia and Arabia swarm with them, and that the inhabitants use them for food. There are some that betake themselves from the fields into houses, and steal money.
